intro: Ivan Ilić plays the Prelude in E minor, Op. 28 No. 4, marked Largo. The melody moves very little over twenty-five bars, and the chords beneath it descend by semitones.

sections.label: A · The chords descend
sections.mNote: Repeated quavers beneath a lingering melody

sections.label: A′ · Opening melody returns, rising to forte
sections.mNote: The opening returns, then rises to a forte.

sections.label: Coda · Rest before E minor
sections.mNote: A held rest separates the last chords.

cues.title: Melody on B, bars 1–4
cues.text: The melody reaches B by an octave leap and stays there, touching C and returning to B. The left hand repeats its chords eight times a bar, and within them individual notes move down by semitones.
cues.evidence: Peters edition, edited by Herrmann Scholtz (1900), upbeat and bars 1–4. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Ivan Ilić, Berkeley and Paris
cues.text: Ilić came to Paris with degrees in mathematics and music from Berkeley, then studied at the Paris Conservatoire and the École Normale. He made this recording in Paris in October 2005. Three years later he released a Debussy disc of that composer’s twenty-four preludes.
cues.evidence: Training and the October 2008 Debussy release: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Ilić_(pianist). Session: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Ivan_Ilić-Chopin_Prelude_Opus_28_n.4.ogg

cues.title: Fermata and final cadence
cues.text: The repeated quavers stop. Chopin puts a fermata over the rest, then marks the final chords pianissimo. In the melody D♯ rises to E while the bass falls from B to E.
cues.evidence: Peters–Scholtz edition, bars 23–25: fermata over the rest, pp, and the final B7–E minor cadence. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: The opening melody returns
transitions.to: A′ · Opening melody returns, rising to forte
transitions.how: A short right-hand flourish crosses the gap left by the accompaniment. At bar 13 the opening B returns over an E minor chord with G in the bass, and the left-hand quavers begin again. This second phrase breaks into stretto at bar 16 and presses forward towards the forte.
transitions.evidence: Peters–Scholtz edition, bars 12–17: accompaniment rests, renewed opening at bar 13, stretto at bar 16. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=921

transitions.title: The quavers stop
transitions.from: A′ · Opening melody returns, rising to forte
transitions.how: The marking smorzando directs the piano to die away. The left-hand quavers stop, a chord is held, and a rest carries a fermata. Three soft chords follow. The last two move from B7 to E minor, with the melody rising D♯–E above B–E in the bass.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
